steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual picture of a Transformer  

1. The problem it solves  
   • We have a sequence of symbols (words, sub-words, pixels, DNA letters, …) and we want a representation that lets the model reason about any part of the sequence while keeping track of the order.  
   • Earlier sequence models (RNNs/LSTMs) scanned tokens one-by-one, so long-range interactions had to flow through many time steps. A Transformer instead looks at the whole sequence at once and lets every position “talk” directly to every other position through attention.  

2. Break the sequence into vectors (tokens)  
   • Each token → an embedding vector e₁ … eₙ.  
   • Add a positional encoding p₁ … pₙ (either fixed sinusoids or learned) and get xᵢ = eᵢ + pᵢ. The model now knows “dog is the 3rd word,” not just “dog.”  

3. Self-attention: the key idea  
   • For every token we create three small vectors produced by learned linear layers:  
     – Query qᵢ “what I’m looking for”  
     – Key   kᵢ “how I can be found”  
     – Value vᵢ “what I carry”  
   • Similarity = dot(qᵢ, kⱼ). After scaling and softmax we get weights αᵢⱼ that say “how much token i attends to token j.”  
   • The new representation for token i is a weighted sum of all values:  
           zᵢ = Σⱼ αᵢⱼ vⱼ  
     Every token now contains information from the whole sentence, but in a way that the model has learned is relevant.  

4. Multi-head attention  
   • Instead of one set of Q, K, V we use h heads (say 8 or 16). Each head learns to focus on different relations: subject-verb agreement, coreference, sub-phrase, etc.  
   • Heads are concatenated and linearly mixed → richer representation.  

5. Feed-forward and residual wiring  
   • After attention we pass z through a small position-wise MLP (two linear layers with ReLU/GEGLU).  
   • Add residual connections (x + attention, then x + MLP) and LayerNorm → stabilizes deep stacks.  

6. Stacking forms an encoder (and a decoder)  
   • Encoder: several identical layers of (self-attention → MLP). Output is a set of contextualized token vectors.  
   • Decoder (for sequence-to-sequence tasks) adds:  
     – Masked self-attention (can’t peek at future tokens).  
     – Encoder-decoder attention (queries come from decoder tokens, keys/values from encoder output) so the decoder can “look back” at the source sentence.  

7. Training objective (example: language modelling)  
   • Masked Language Model (BERT-style): hide some tokens and predict them.  
   • Auto-regressive (GPT-style): predict next token given past tokens.  
   • Sequence-to-sequence (T5, original Transformer): predict target sentence given source sentence.  
   Gradients flow through attention, so the network learns what relations matter.  

8. Why it works conceptually  
   • Global receptive field in one hop: any token can influence any other.  
   • Parallelizable: all tokens processed simultaneously, unlike RNNs.  
   • Multi-head = multiple, interpretable relation detectors.  
   • Deep stacking lets later layers build on earlier discovered relations.  

9. Inference time  
   • Encoder-only model: feed sequence once, get contextual embeddings or logits.  
   • Decoder-only (GPT): generate token-by-token; at each step recompute or cache keys/values so generation is fast.  

10. Mental analogy  
   Imagine reading a sentence and, for every word, you draw arrows to every other word with thickness proportional to “how much this word matters to me.” Then you rewrite the sentence where each word is now a blended summary of all the words it cared about. Stack this operation repeatedly—each pass lets the model see higher-order relations (noun ↔ verb ↔ clause ↔ document).  

Key takeaway  
A Transformer is just repeated layers of “look at everything (attention), decide what matters (softmax weights), blend information (weighted sum), re-mix through a feed-forward network, and keep the original information around (residuals).” This simple, fully parallel block, plus positional clues, turns out to be a very powerful universal pattern-recognizer for sequences.
